newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Fierce clashes could restart Angola civil war.
newsitem.headline: Fierce clashes could restart Angola civil war.

text.p: Angolan troops are running into fierce resistance from heavily armed soldiers of the former rebel movement UNITA in a flareup of fighting in the diamond-rich northeast which threatens to restart civil war.
Diplomats said the fighting, the heaviest since since the rivals signed a ceasefire in 1994 to end 20 years of conflict, could derail Angola's fragile peace process.
Ironically, the former foes sat together only this week in the country's first national unity parliament.
But analysts say UNITA is split between those seeking reconciliation and hardline generals in the bush, including UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi.

In a domino effect from the upheaval in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, UNITA has also lost the key backing of ousted president Mobutu Sese Seko, long a vital supporter.

UNITA, which still controls most of the countryside and 80 percent of the lucrative diamond fields, was strongly resisting a government army bid to oust it from the region, according to a senior military source in the capital, Luanda.
He said UNITA might have thrown up to "six and seven battalions" into the battle. Government troops were using tanks, artillery and anti-aircraft cannon.
Relief workers earlier reported seeing about 70 wounded government soldiers being treated at a local hospital, but had no word on UNITA casualties.

The precarious peacetime balance between the Angolan government and UNITA, who were armed by Soviet allies and the West respectively during the Cold War, was upset last month when Mobutu was toppled from power.
Mobutu, who ruled Zaire for 32 years, was ousted by the rebel army of Laurent Kabila, who enjoys the active support of the Angolan government of President Jose Eduardo dos Santos.

The government army advanced into UNITA turf almost as soon as Kabila installed himself as president last month, evidently determined to undo the logistical structure Zaire had provided for UNITA, including routes used to ship out diamonds.
The military source in Luanda told Reuters that the government had taken three towns -- Canzar, Cambulo and Tchitotolo -- which they found deserted.

Moving south from Nzage, however, they met strong resistance at Mbuia, Cossa and Maludi where fighting was still continuing. "Resistance was so heavy it might have included between six and seven battalions on UNITA's side," he added.
The Angolan army were coming under mortar fire, causing heavy casualties. They had lost three troop carriers, and captured a truck with a Zairean number plate.

The source said government forces under the leadership of military chief General Joao de Matos were seeking to cut off main routes used by UNITA to smuggle diamonds into former Zaire, now renamed the Democratic Republic of Congo.
The Congolese town of Kamina was used by UNITA as a supply base for its diamond area, but was deserted in February this year when Kabila's troops swept across the country.
Aid workers said thousands of civilians had fled villages in the northeast as the fighting intensified, making for the safety of government-controlled Nzage, a diamond mining town.
They quoted villagers as saying many civilians had been killed in three weeks of clashes.

"The number of internally displaced are being registered and the figure is at around 3,500. We've been told to expect more because of fighting," a U.N. relief official told Reuters after returning from a visit to the region this week.
"The people coming into Nzage saying the war has started again and civilians are being killed."
